questions.question: Explain two weaknesses of the League of Nations. (4 marks)

points.text: The League had no army of its own - it could not enforce decisions militarily and had to rely on member states to provide troops, who often refused. The unanimity rule meant that any Council member could veto action, so a single "no" vote could prevent the League from responding to aggression.

questions.question: How important was America's absence from the League of Nations? (8 marks)

points.text: America's absence was critically important. Without the USA, the League lacked the world's most powerful economy and military. Economic sanctions were weaker without American trade; other powers knew the League could not call on American support; and the League's moral authority was undermined. questions.question: "The League of Nations was a complete failure." How far do you agree? (12 marks)

points.text: The League was NOT a complete failure. In the 1920s, it successfully resolved disputes (Aaland Islands 1921, Greece-Bulgaria 1925, Upper Silesia 1921). Its humanitarian work was genuinely impressive: Nansen helped 425,000 refugees; the ILO improved working conditions; the Health Organisation combatted disease; and 200,000 slaves were freed. questions.question: Explain why the League was more successful in the 1920s than the 1930s. (8 marks)

points.text: The League was more successful in the 1920s because: the international climate was more cooperative (Locarno Spring); the disputes involved small nations who could not defy the League; the major powers supported League decisions because it suited their interests; and the economic prosperity reduced tensions. points.text: The humanitarian work was certainly impressive: the Health Organisation, ILO, Nansen's refugee work, anti-slavery campaigns, and drug control all achieved real results that outlasted the League itself.
